discipline: vision science / eye-tracking psychophysiology and methodology; empirically-derived reporting-guideline review (STEM-methods)
thesis: Reviewing the empirical literature on how instrument, methodology, environment, and participant factors affect eye-tracking data quality (accuracy, precision, data loss, latency) and downstream eye-movement/gaze measures, and comparing this evidence base against five existing reporting guidelines and a 207-study reporting-practices database, the authors show that current reporting guidelines vary substantially and do not match actual reporting practice. They derive a flexible, minimal reporting guideline -- distinguished explicitly from a mandatory reporting standard -- comprising a full item catalogue (Table 6), a 9-item strongly-recommended minimal core (Table 7), and context-specific supplementary checklists (Tables 8-18). A full-text search of the extracted source confirms zero occurrences of 'boredom,' 'boring,' or 'monotony'; the paper is purely methodological and contains no construct-level engagement with boredom whatsoever.

sections.title: Abstract / Introduction / Structure of this paper
sections.summary: States the empirical-vs-reporting-practice gap, previews the three evidentiary bases (scoping review, five guidelines, 207-study database), and introduces Table 1's term glossary.

sections.title: Measuring data quality of eye-tracker signals
sections.summary: Table 1 term glossary (P-CR, DPI, EOG, scleral coil, limbus, retinal tracking, calibration, gaze direction/position, sampling frequency, accuracy, precision, resolution, data loss, system latency, event detection, AOI); operationalizations and formulas for accuracy, precision (RMS-S2S, STD), data loss, and system latency.

sections.title: A review of empirical eye-tracking studies as the basis for a reporting guideline
sections.summary: The paper's long central section: eye-tracking methods and their differences (Table 2, 42 benchmarking studies); environment (pupil-size artefact, vibration, presence of others, MRI, VR); setup and geometry; participants (age, clinical groups, arousal/workload/pupil dilation, sleep deprivation, expertise, pathology/personality, medication); calibration and accuracy; signal properties and processing (sampling frequency, precision, filters); fixation and saccade detection (event-detection algorithms); AOI measures; higher-order measures; summary.

sections.title: Reporting practices and existing reporting guidelines
sections.summary: Actual reporting rates from the 207-study database (Table 4) compared against five existing guidelines (Fiedler et al. 2019; Carter & Luke 2020; McConkie 1981; Oakes 2010; Strohmaier et al. 2020); concludes guidelines are incomplete, inconsistent, and field-biased.

sections.title: An empirically based minimal reporting guideline
sections.summary: Table 6 (full reporting-item catalogue by section with examples/units/exemplar citations); Table 7 (the paper's own 9-item minimal core); Tables 8-18 (context-specific supplementary checklists for clinical studies, wearable/unconstrained recording, pupil-size estimation, AOI research, multi-screen setups, gaze-contingent research, saccade reaction-time studies, etc.).

sections.title: Open Practices Statement / Conclusions
sections.summary: Notes the 207-study reporting database's public availability; restates that reporting is negotiated case-by-case and proposes the flexible guideline as a corrective.

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: not named as such; the Arousal, mental fatigue and cognitive workload subsection reviews pupil dilation, blink rate, and microsaccade dynamics as indices of reduced task engagement under fatigue/low arousal; 'attentional disengagement' appears once verbatim in an unrelated ASD gaze-behaviour context (Keehn et al., 2013)

constructs.label: mind-wandering / task-unrelated thought
constructs.treatment: not named; the same arousal/fatigue subsection's account of degraded oculomotor engagement under low arousal is the nearest functional analogue, via our own bridge, not the source's claim

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: not treated as boredom; analogically present via the cited Van Orden et al. (2000) surveillance-tracking (vigilance) task combining fixation duration, blink duration, and pupil dilation as a repetitive-task performance predictor

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: one incidental mention ('participant performance and engagement') as a rationale for retaining manual eye-tracking data coding; not developed as a construct

constructs.label: profound/deep boredom (FCM 3rd form); being-bored-by (1st form); being-bored-with (2nd form); situational vs. trait/state boredom; boredom proneness; boredom-as-regulatory-signal (functional account); temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: not treated; no vocabulary or citation contact with any of these constructs exists anywhere in the 53pp source (confirmed via full-text search for 'boredom,' 'boring,' 'monotony')

measures.label: pupil dilation / pupillometry
measures.signal: pupil diameter/area in the eye-camera image (most P-CR trackers do not report physical pupil size); systematically affected by two artefacts -- the pupil-size artefact (illumination-driven constriction/dilation altering the gaze estimate itself) and the pupil-foreshortening artefact (off-axis gaze deforming imaged pupil shape, shortening measured diameter)
measures.apparatus: any P-CR video-based tracker; artefact compensation via geometric modelling (Gagl et al., 2011) or artificial-eye-based correction (Hayes & Petrov, 2016); calibration across a range of pupil sizes recommended when stimulus luminance varies
measures.sample_n: N/A (methodological review synthesizing many cited studies, not a single-sample empirical study)
measures.key_result: Mental workload and arousal positively associated with pupil dilation across a large controlled-study literature (Kahneman & Beatty 1966; Ahern & Beatty 1979; Hess & Polt 1964; Einhäuser 2017); flagged as 'of particular importance for experiments using the pupil size as a measurement for estimates of the participant's psychological state (e.g. cognitive load or arousal)' (FAITHFUL-Holmqvist et al., p.379)

measures.label: gaze variance / fixation dispersion
measures.signal: spatial dispersion of gaze-position samples during fixation, operationalized via RMS-S2S (Eq. 1, noise-velocity indicator), STD or BCEA (dispersion indicators), and the I-DT algorithm's dispersion threshold (typically 0.75-1.5° spatial, 50-150ms temporal)
measures.apparatus: any eye tracker; precision/dispersion calculations following Niehorster et al.'s (2020c) four-measure framework (RMS-S2S, STD, BCEA, power-spectrum-slope 'noise colour')
measures.key_result: Precision distributions vary by roughly two orders of magnitude between eye-tracker models (Holmqvist & Andersson, 2017); AOI dwell-time and gaze-transition-entropy measures built atop dispersion/fixation data show large, non-linear sensitivity to AOI size and event-detector settings (Hessels et al. 2016; Krejtz et al. 2015)

measures.label: blink / eye-closure
measures.signal: blink rate and blink duration, plus their contribution to data loss (~2% of total data per Holmqvist & Andersson, 2017, p.167)
measures.apparatus: any eye tracker with blink/eye-closure detection; dedicated 'blink algorithm' entries surveyed in the reporting-practices comparison (Table 4/5)
measures.key_result: Blink-rate findings under cognitive workload are mixed and task-dependent: some studies (Recarte et al. 2008; Čegovnik et al. 2018) report increases with workload, others (Bauer et al. 1987; Fogarty & Stern 1989) report decreases, and Brouwer et al. (2014) found no effect

measures.label: behavioral (RT / errors / performance-monitoring)
measures.signal: saccadic latency, antisaccade error/direction-error rate, and reaction-time-adjacent gaze-contingent timing measures
measures.apparatus: gaze-contingent and saccade-reaction-time paradigms; a dedicated context-specific checklist (Table 18) covers stimulus-display latency quantification for these designs
measures.key_result: Sleep deprivation, benzodiazepines, and cannabis increase saccadic latency and antisaccade error rates while nicotine reduces them; schizophrenia and related conditions show large, reliable oculomotor performance-monitoring impairments (reduced smooth-pursuit gain, increased antisaccade direction errors)

measures.label: ML classification
measures.signal: end-to-end learned event classification of fixations, saccades, and post-saccadic oscillations directly from raw gaze signal, without hand-coded velocity/dispersion rules
measures.apparatus: GazeNet (Zemblys et al., 2019) and the Deep eye movement classifier (Startsev et al., 2019, which additionally detects smooth pursuit); benchmarked against human expert coders rather than ground-truth rules
measures.key_result: Machine-learning event detectors achieve 'very high resemblance to human expert coders'; the paper notes an unresolved methodological debate over what should count as ground truth (human coding vs. rule-based algorithms) when validating such classifiers

measures.label: heart rate / HRV (comparative citation only, not this paper's own measure)
measures.signal: cited once, comparatively, not measured by this paper itself
measures.key_result: Eye-movement measures of cognitive load found more sensitive than heart-rate, skin, and brain (EEG) measures across the meta-study -- a cross-modal sensitivity ranking directly relevant to any dataset instrumenting both EEG and eye-tracking channels

readings.claim: Reporting practices diverge sharply from what the empirical review shows matters: only 12.5% of 207 surveyed studies report the recording environment, while eye-tracker model (90.8%) and sampling frequency (75.8%) are commonly reported despite mattering less in most cases than data quality.
Existing reporting guidelines 'differ substantially from one another,' are based on small-group consensus rather than this paper's empirical review, and are not widely used.
Existing guidelines are incomplete and inconsistent, and often biased towards specific research fields.

A minimal, strongly-recommended reporting core (Table 7) comprises nine items: eye-tracker technique; empirically-determined sampling frequency; setup/geometry with head-stabilization details; recording environment; participant instructions; empirically-determined data quality (gaze and pupil signals); processing/analysis-step description with parameters; firmware/software versions; and exclusion criteria.

A single, one-size-fits-all reporting checklist is counterproductive because not all aspects in the full item catalogue (Table 6) are relevant to every study; the guideline should instead help authors make an informed selection.

Reporting guidelines (informed-choice recommendations) are conceptually distinct from reporting standards (mandatory, authority-approved requirements); this paper deliberately delivers the empirical foundation and the former, not the latter.

Degrading precision from 0.03 deg to 0.37 deg increased mean fixation duration from 430ms to 630ms and reduced the number of detected fixations by roughly one-third on the same underlying eye-movement data.

Precision in VR-integrated eye trackers (SMI Vive goggles) is significantly poorer than in glasses-based tracking, though accuracy differs only in some conditions; VR headset end-to-end latency ranges roughly 45-81ms.
readings.stance: reports (Pastel et al. 2021; Stein et al. 2021, cited)

readings.claim: Eye-movement measures of cognitive load are more sensitive than heart-rate, skin, and brain (EEG) measures across a 33-experiment meta-study.

Controlled studies of the effect of environmental vibrations on eye-tracking data quality appear to be lacking; very few studies examine how changing event-detector settings or data quality affects higher-order measures.

interlocutors.name: Carter, Benjamin T., & Luke, Steven G. (2020)
interlocutors.role: one of five existing guidelines compared; unique among them in requesting demographic information and dependent-variable-selection justification

interlocutors.name: McConkie, George W. (1981)
interlocutors.role: earliest-cited call for eye-tracking reporting guidance; recommended event-detection algorithm details be published in the presenting paper

interlocutors.name: Oakes, Lisa M. (2010)
interlocutors.role: one of five existing reporting guidelines compared

interlocutors.name: Strohmaier, A. R., et al. (2020)
interlocutors.role: one of five existing reporting guidelines compared

interlocutors.name: Salvucci, Dario D., & Goldberg, Joseph H. (2000)
interlocutors.role: originators of the I-DT and I-VT fixation/saccade detection algorithms, foundational to nearly all subsequent event-detection software

interlocutors.name: Nyström, Marcus, & Holmqvist, Kenneth (2010)
interlocutors.role: NH2010 noise-adaptive event-detection algorithm with post-saccadic-oscillation output; also source of the precision-degradation fixation-duration finding

interlocutors.name: Hessels, Roy S., et al. (2017)
interlocutors.role: I2MC algorithm, designed for robustness to noise and data loss common in infant eye-tracking research

interlocutors.name: Zemblys, Raimondas, et al. (2019)
interlocutors.role: GazeNet, a fully end-to-end machine-learning event detector matching human expert coders

interlocutors.name: Niehorster, Diederick C., et al. (2020c)
interlocutors.role: four-measure precision framework (RMS-S2S, STD, BCEA, power-spectrum slope), cited throughout the data-quality sections

interlocutors.name: Holmqvist, Kenneth, & Andersson, Richard (2017)
interlocutors.role: the authors' own eye-tracking methodology textbook, the paper's single most frequently cited background reference throughout

interlocutors.name: Ayres, Paul, et al. (2021)
interlocutors.role: 33-experiment meta-study finding eye-movement measures of cognitive load more sensitive than heart-rate, skin, and EEG measures

interlocutors.name: Pastel, Stefan, et al. (2021)
interlocutors.role: found significantly poorer precision in VR-integrated (SMI Vive) eye trackers compared to glasses-based tracking

interlocutors.name: Stein, Nikolas, et al. (2021)
interlocutors.role: measured 45-81ms end-to-end latency across common VR headsets

interlocutors.name: Kahneman, Daniel, & Beatty, Jackson (1966)
interlocutors.role: foundational demonstration that pupil dilation tracks memory-task load, cited as the origin of the pupil-dilation/cognitive-load literature

interlocutors.name: Van Orden, Kevin F., et al. (2000)
interlocutors.role: regression model combining fixation duration, blink duration, and mean pupil dilation into a robust predictor of surveillance-tracking-task (vigilance) performance

interlocutors.name: Open Science Collaboration (2015)
interlocutors.role: estimate that only about one-third of psychology findings replicate, the paper's motivating 'replication crisis' citation

tensions.axis: reporting guideline (flexible, informed-choice) vs. reporting standard (mandatory, authority-approved)
tensions.note: the paper's own explicit conceptual distinction; it deliberately delivers only the empirical foundation and the former, while suggesting its findings could later seed the latter.

tensions.axis: what the empirical literature shows matters for data quality vs. what researchers actually report
tensions.note: the paper's central diagnostic axis, evidenced by the 207-study database comparison (e.g. only 12.5% report environment despite documented large environmental effects).

tensions.axis: single universal checklist vs. flexible, study-type-dependent reporting structure
tensions.note: the paper explicitly rejects prior guidelines' single-list approach in favor of a full catalogue (Table 6) plus minimal core (Table 7) plus context-specific supplements (Tables 8-18).

tensions.axis: eye-tracking measures of cognitive load vs. EEG/heart-rate/skin measures (cross-modal sensitivity)
tensions.note: Ayres et al. (2021), cited here, ranks eye-tracking above EEG/heart/skin for cognitive-load sensitivity -- a live methodological consideration for this cluster's Strand D (EEG-centric) versus Strand E (eye-tracking) framing of boredom's physiological signature, though the source itself makes no boredom-specific claim (P/anticipatory-application).
